newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK rates glued to the spot until election.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK rates glued to the spot until election.

text.p: The chances of official British interest rates rising this week are close to zero, economists said on Monday. A Reuter poll of 21 London-based economists forecast a base rate rise after May 1 elections, regardless of who wins, but none expected a monetary tightening before the vote.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George hold their monthly monetary meeting on Thursday. Flying pigs and a world-beating England cricket team were both touted as more likely than a rate increase this week.

"Monetary policy is seemingly frozen in the headlights of the general election, and it would be truly staggering if Mr Clarke opted to put economics before politics," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
But George will still push for a tightening, as he has consistently in recent months, he said.
Neil Parker, economist at The Royal Bank of Scotland agreed it would be "absolutely incredible" if Clarke raised rates just before the election.

But with annual average earnings growing at five percent, strong retail sales and consumer credit growth and core inflation well above the government's 2.5 percent target -- it was 2.9 percent year-on-year in February -- George may push for a half-point rate rise at the first monetary meeting after the election, Parker said.

The short sterling strip is pricing in a half-point rate rise by the end of June. Less than a month ago, it was discounting only a quarter-point rise but that was before another large drop in unemployment in February accompanied a leap in annual wages growth to five percent.

In a televised debate with his opposition counterparts Gordon Brown and Malcolm Bruce on Sunday, Clarke said underlying inflation would drop below the government's 2.5 percent target this year and said the difference of opinion between him and George amounted to just 1/4 of a percentage point.
Last week, George acknowledged a rate rise would hit UK exporters, already squeezed by a 20 percent rise by the pound against core European currencies over the last six months.
But he said the pace of domestic demand required some monetary tightening. At all monetary meetings this year, George has pressed for rates to be raised from six percent.

Garrard said rising average earnings and strong growth in broad money supply was still offset by an absence of pipeline inflation pressures. Output prices rose just 1.3 percent in the year to February.

But he forecast an incoming Labour Chancellor would establish his anti-inflationary credentials by raising rates soon after the election. Base rates would be at 6.75 percent by the end of the year, he said.
Labour, with a commanding lead of 20 points and more in the polls, is poised to take power for the first time in 18 years.
For Clarke, Thursday's meeting may be a poignant occasion. If the polls are right, his chances of still being Chancellor after May 1 look decidedly slim.

"The Chancellor's never-say-die spirit will not allow him to concede that this will be the last ever-performance in the long-running Ken-and-Eddie show," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking. "But it would not be surprising if an end-of-term atmosphere prevailed."
